definition: The set of assumptions a learning algorithm uses to make predictions on inputs it hasn't specifically seen before.
details: Inductive bias is built into model architecture choices — for example, convolutional networks assume spatial locality matters, while transformers make comparatively fewer built-in assumptions about input structure, relying more on data to learn such patterns.

explainer.lead: Inductive bias is what lets a model generalize to inputs it never saw; without some assumption about how the world works, no learner could predict anything on new data. The strength of that bias shapes whether a model learns fast from little data or needs far more data to discover structure on its own.

tiers.eli5: It's like a student who walks into class already assuming that things close together tend to be related — that head start helps them learn faster than someone with no assumptions at all.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers pick architectures to bake in the bias that matches the data: convolutions for images, sequence models for text. The pitfall is too strong a bias — a model that assumes the wrong structure will fail no matter how much data you throw at it.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, inductive bias is the set of assumptions an algorithm uses to predict outputs for inputs not present in training, and it is a property of the architecture and hypothesis space, not the data. No universal bias fits all problems; a bias that helps on one task can hurt on another.

explainer.example: A convolutional network assumes nearby pixels matter to each other, so it learns image features from modest data; a transformer makes fewer such assumptions and typically needs more data to reach the same accuracy on images.
